reading_purpose.why_this_paper_was_pulled: It was flagged as a threat to ch25's self-contribution claim: ch25 positions 'the book's unified cost accounting' (experiment X1) as the book's own contribution, and this paper announces a phase-aware profiler attributing cost to construction, retrieval and generation. The four questions this note must settle are (a) what is actually measured and in what UNITS, (b) which of the book's four cost cells $B_s$/$L_w$/$C_{\text{cap}}$/$\rho$ it fills, (c) whether its 'amortization via query volume' is identity (A) and whether it counts the PREFILL term, and (d) what of ch25's contribution survives and what moves to prior art.
reading_purpose.answer_in_one_line: It fills three of the four cells with real measurements on ten $E$-path systems, it counts prefill thoroughly on the WRITE path and only as latency on the READ path, it never writes an amortisation identity and never varies $N_q$ — so ch25's judgement 2 survives intact while ch25's framing, its priority claim on phase attribution, and ch26's $E$-path byte ordering all take damage.

problem_stated.as_the_paper_frames_it: 'A rich ecosystem of agent memory systems has emerged spanning flat retrieval, LLM-mediated extraction, consolidating fact stores, and agentic control flows. Yet, their system-level behavior remains uncharacterized. We present the first systems characterization of agent memory.' [agent-mem-sys Abstract, p.1]
problem_stated.the_gap_it_names: 'Existing benchmarks evaluate these systems purely on downstream accuracy [6, 14, 27, 28], leaving their system-level behavior uncharacterized. Yet, these design choices drastically and asymmetrically redistribute cost: a system that compresses history into atomic facts slashes query-time prompt length but pays orders-of-magnitude more in construction-time LLM prefill; a graph-based memory improves relational retrieval while multiplying embedding traffic and storage footprint. These costs are invisible to accuracy metrics, yet critically dominate at deployment scale.' [agent-mem-sys §1, p.2]
three_research_questions: 'What are the key tradeoffs among emerging paradigms for constructing and using memory in long-horizon agent workloads?' [§1, p.2]
'What computational costs and system opportunities do these workloads expose, and what demands do they place on deployment infrastructure?' [§1, p.2]

'How do specific algorithmic design choices concerning the construction mechanism, storage organization, retrieval policy, and update strategy shape observable system characteristics such as utilization, bandwidth, latency, and scalability?' [§1, p.2]
problem_stated.note_writer_remark: [note-writer] The gap this paper names is, almost verbatim, the gap ch25 names — 'costs are invisible to accuracy metrics'. The difference is method: this paper closes it by MEASUREMENT on ten deployed systems; ch25 closes it by CLOSED-FORM ACCOUNTING on one published cost model. The two are not the same object and neither subsumes the other, but the book can no longer present the question itself as unasked.

inherited_open_question.verdict: none-stated, and the silence is structural rather than accidental
inherited_open_question.justification: The paper quotes no prior work's open question. Its §1 lineage statement is a technique progression, not a handed-forward problem: 'Early systems treated knowledge as purely parametric, encoded in model weights at training time. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) decoupled knowledge from parameters by attaching LLMs to static external corpora... Long-horizon agents extend this further: the memory corpus is no longer a fixed document collection that is preprocessed and indexed a priori, but a mutable state produced by the agent's own interaction stream' [§1, pp.1-2]. The 'first systems characterization' framing manufactures the gap by pointing at what accuracy benchmarks do not measure, exactly as [letta-stc] manufactured its gap by pointing at an assumption inside the test-time-scaling literature.

inherited_open_question.bridge_material_for_the_book: [note-writer] This paper is the empirical answer to a question ch25 raises and then declares unanswerable from the corpus — 'what is $B_s$?'. It answers it for ten $E$-path systems in Joules, calls and wall-clock. ch25 must therefore stop saying the question is unanswerable and start saying that the SLEEP-TIME-COMPUTE papers do not answer it while the systems community, working under a different name, does.

core_mechanism.one_line_unified: The paper introduces no update rule. It introduces a MEASUREMENT INSTRUMENT — a phase-aware profiling harness that splits an agent-memory execution into construction / retrieval / generation and attributes tokens, calls, wall-clock, GPU counters and integrated device energy to each phase — plus a four-axis taxonomy of $E$-path write and read paths.

what_it_establishes: The discriminant applied to a ten-system 2026 systems study returns 7/10 — a completely different rate from the 0/47 the same test returned on the architecture-side survey (`memory-survey-2607`). Read together, the two results say the category is dense in the AGENT-MEMORY literature and empty in the ARCHITECTURE-MEMORY literature. That is a sharper statement than ch11 currently makes and it belongs in ch24.

The two systems that FAIL — BM25 and embedRAG — are the top two on accuracy in the paper's macro-average (55.8% and 50.3%) [§4.5, Fig. 7a, p.9]. The discriminant's exclusion line and the accuracy ranking's top line coincide. This is the single strongest external evidence in the whole corpus for ch27 판정 2.

Six of the seven passers are NEW to the book's corpus (GraphRAG, HippoRAG v2, SimpleMem, A-Mem, Letta-as-product, MIRIX). The book's 9-passer count is a count of PAPERS IT READ, not a census of the category, and ch24 should say so.

rho.value: ABSENT — and the paper states the reason.
rho.detail: 'None of the evaluated systems prune or forget by default, so footprint grows monotonically under default behavior; bounding fleet storage requires an independent forgetting policy' [§4.7, p.10]. 'In many current systems, maintenance is weak or absent: memory accumulates indefinitely with no freshness or pruning policy, which becomes critical for long-lived agents where state grows continuously and may become redundant or stale' [§2.1, p.3]. No repeated-consolidation experiment exists; there is no round index anywhere in the paper.
adjacent_quantities_that_are_NOT_rho: STALENESS — 'the number of prior sessions not yet persisted to the memory store at query time; a system is fresh when staleness is zero' [§4.6, p.9]. Measured: max stale 1 or 2 for SimpleMem, MIRIX, Letta, Mem0, A-Mem under a 5 s inter-session gap; BM25 and embedRAG stay fresh in both modes [Fig. 8b, p.9]. This is a scheduling lag, not a per-round quality loss.
The MemoryAgentBench 'selective forgetting' family (FactConsolidation-SH/MH) scores in Fig. 7b (p.9). These are task accuracies at a single pass, not a decay rate over rounds.
'marginal per-chunk construction cost' rising as stores grow [Recommendation 8, p.9] and the super-linear token-cost growth of Paradigm IV [Insight 7, p.10]. Both are COST growth, not quality decay.
rho.book_reading: ch25's $\rho$ row ('**0편**', 'measured되지 않은 것이 아니라 측정될 실험이 설계되지 않았다') is CONFIRMED by an independent source at ten-system scale, and the paper supplies a mechanism-level reason: the operator that would produce $\rho$ (maintenance/forgetting) is not implemented by default in ANY of the ten systems. That is a stronger statement than the book currently has and ch25/ch30 should take it.

N_q.detail: LongMemEval_S_* 'contains five samples, each with approximately 360K tokens of history and 60 queries (300 total)' [§3.1, p.4]. Every cost total in the paper is Construct + 300 QA at that fixed 60-queries-per-context. MemoryArena's physics split is 20 multi-session tasks, one query per session. No distribution of $N_q$ from any real workload appears.
N_q.book_reading: ch25 §25.3.3's claim — '실서빙에서 한 문맥을 몇 개 질의가 공유하는지의 분포를 보고한 논문이 corpus에 없다' — survives, and this paper is a fresh instance of the same defect from a systems venue that had every instrument needed to measure it.

what_it_does_NOT_measure: QA-PHASE TOKENS. Fig. 5 has (a.i) construction calls, (a.ii) construction GPU traffic, (b) QA phase CALLS per query, (c) construction TOKENS. There is no QA-phase token decomposition anywhere in the paper. Read-path prefill therefore appears only as seconds (effective TTFT, Fig. 10) and never as a token count. THIS IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT ABSENCE FOR ch25 — see amortization_analysis.
Any $W$-path or $\Theta$-path system. The 'first systems characterization of agent memory' covers external stores only.
Dollar cost. Energy is the operator-facing currency throughout; no pricing, no $\kappa_{\text{cost}}$-equivalent.
Accuracy variance. No error bars, seeds, confidence intervals or dispersion statistics appear anywhere, on n=5 samples (LongMemEval) and n=20 tasks (MemoryArena).

amortization_analysis.question: Is the paper's 'amortization via query volume' the book's identity (A), and does it count the prefill term?
amortization_analysis.where_the_phrase_occurs: TWICE, both in front matter, and nowhere else in the paper. Abstract: 'we derive 10 system recommendations covering construction scheduling, capability floors, amortization via query volume, freshness-latency tradeoffs, and fleet-scale management' [Abstract, p.1]. Contributions bullet: 'A comprehensive systems characterization spanning construction cost shape, capability thresholds, amortization structure, freshness scheduling, footprint growth, and retrieval tail behavior' [§1, p.2]. A whole-text grep for 'amorti' returns exactly these two lines.

what_the_body_actually_delivers.the_realised_recommendation: Recommendation 6, §4.5 (p.8), in full: 'Operators selecting an agent memory system should match the construction-versus-query cost split to the workload's query arrival pattern, in addition to matching the agent memory system's capability profile to the dominant task family. High-volume query workloads against stable histories favor agent memory systems that move work into construction. Continuous-ingestion workloads with sparse queries favor agent memory systems with low construction costs.'
what_the_body_actually_delivers.verdict_on_form: This is identity (A) stated in PROSE and in DIRECTION only. There is no equation in the paper — zero numbered equations, the same structural absence the book recorded for [letta-stc]. There is no symbol for the number of queries per context, no break-even quantity, no crossover curve, no $N_q$ sweep, no algebra of any kind.
what_the_body_actually_delivers.the_one_point_at_which_A_is_evaluated: Table 3 (p.6) is $C_{\text{sleep}} + N_q\,C_{\text{wake}}$ evaluated at exactly one $N_q$ (60 queries per context; 300 queries over 5 contexts) for nine systems, in Joules. A reader can divide and get $C_{\text{avg}}$; the paper never does. The three quantities identity (A) needs are all present in Table 3 and Fig. 3 (construction energy, per-query QA energy, query count) and are never assembled.
what_the_body_actually_delivers.insight_2_is_the_amortisation_result_in_: 'Construction energy dominates the agent lifecycle: for LLM-mediated agent memory systems, construction energy exceeds total query-phase energy across 300 queries' [Insight 2, p.6]. Read through identity (A) this says $C_{\text{sleep}}/N_q > C_{\text{wake}}$ at $N_q = 300$ for the LLM-mediated systems — i.e. the break-even is BEYOND 300 queries per five contexts for those systems. The paper states the inequality and never names it as a break-even. [본서 추론]

does_it_count_the_prefill_term.write_path: YES, thoroughly, in tokens. Section 4.3 is titled 'Construction Is an Overwhelmingly Embedding and Prefill-dominated Workload' (p.7). 'Construction is dominated by embedding and LLM prefill: the embedding model's entire forward pass is prefill with no decode component, and the LLM construction path reads a window or chunk and emits a compact structured output... whose token count is small relative to the context consumed. The median decode share of total construction tokens is 4.6%... Construction is a repeated long-read, short-write workload.' [§4.3, p.7]. Fig. 5c decomposes construction tokens into Prefill (LLM Prompt) / Decode (LLM Completion) / Embed Input.
does_it_count_the_prefill_term.read_path: PARTIALLY, and only in seconds. The paper names read-path prefill precisely — prompt assembly is the stage 'yielding the prefill length of the final answer-generation call' [§2.1, p.3] — and its whole motivation for external memory is bounding it: 'prefill costs scale quadratically with history length. Prefix caching mitigates this within active sessions but fails across sessions due to cache eviction and the massive KV-cache memory pressure placed on the serving stack' [§1, p.2]; 'By persisting state externally and retrieving only a query-relevant subset, they bound per-query prefill costs' [§1, p.2]. But no QA-phase token decomposition exists. Per-query prefill is observable only as effective TTFT in seconds (Fig. 10, p.10) and as total per-query latency.
does_it_count_the_prefill_term.inside_an_amortisation_identity: NEVER. There is no identity. The per-query prompt cost is never divided by anything and never set against the once-per-context cost in a single expression.

verdict_for_ch25_and_X1.what_X1_still_owns: X1's object is the UNDIVIDED PER-QUERY PREFILL TERM inside identity (A) — $w_{\text{in}}\kappa_{\parallel}|\hat c|$ in ch25 식 (25-1) — and the two quantities it generates, the threshold length $L^\ast$ (식 25-2) beyond which no $N_q$ can win, and the break-even $N_q^\ast$ (식 25-3) that diverges as $|\hat c| \to L^\ast$. This paper contains none of that: no identity, no threshold, no divergence, and no read-path token count from which the term could be built. ch25 판정 2 is untouched.
verdict_for_ch25_and_X1.what_X1_no_longer_owns: The PREMISE that motivated it. ch25 §25.3.1 argues '항이 빠진 것은 우연이 아니라 구조다' and treats the generated-token axis as the field's blind spot. As of 2026-06-04 the systems community's headline finding is that the generated-token axis misses ~95% of write-path cost (median decode share 4.6%). The blind spot is specific to the sleep-time-compute papers, not to the field, and ch25 must say which.
verdict_for_ch25_and_X1.the_honest_line_to_draw: [note-writer] Draw it at the PHASE. This paper prices the WRITE path in tokens and the READ path in seconds. X1 prices the READ path in tokens and puts it in the identity. Those are complementary, not competing, and the sentence ch25 needs is one sentence: 'the systems literature measures construction prefill and the sleep-time literature measures wake decode; nobody has put wake prefill into the amortisation identity, and that is what X1 does.' That sentence is defensible and is much narrower than what ch25 currently implies.

workloads.why_chosen: 'the most widely adopted long-term conversational memory setting in MAB... cleanly separating construction over a long interaction history from repeated query-time retrieval and generation'

headline_numbers.claim: Query-time latency spans two orders of magnitude across systems on identical hardware, and external memory beats long-context serving by a wide margin
headline_numbers.exact_wording: 'Most agent memory systems serve queries in a fraction of long-context wall time while matching or exceeding its accuracy: Mem0 achieves <0.1 s per query versus ~38 s for long-context (GPT-4.1-mini, OpenAI API, averaged over 300 queries)... Fig. 2 shows two orders of magnitude spread in per-query latency across systems on (local) identical hardware.'
headline_numbers.caveat: the <0.1 s figure is in tension with §4.5's ~2.2 s macro-average for Mem0 and with Fig. 10's 0.57 s total; see unfavorable_facts

headline_numbers.claim: Construction energy dominates the agent lifecycle
headline_numbers.exact_wording: 'Construction energy dominates the agent lifecycle: for LLM-mediated agent memory systems, construction energy exceeds total query-phase energy across 300 queries. Energy per correct answer exceeds 47x across the suite, and agent memory systems with similar accuracy can differ by an order of magnitude on this axis.'
headline_numbers.numbers: end-to-end energy 582 kJ (BM25) to 15,429 kJ (Letta), stated as 'over 26.7x' (printed values give 26.5x); J/correct 4,128 to 185,873 (printed values give 45.0x, not 47x)

headline_numbers.exact_wording: 'The median decode share of total construction tokens is 4.6% across agent memory systems, ranging from 0.9% (Letta) to 28.5% (SimpleMem, whose per-window memory entries are longer). Construction is a repeated long-read, short-write workload.'

headline_numbers.claim: Embedding traffic is bimodal by paradigm
headline_numbers.exact_wording: 'GraphRAG yields ~2,300 sequences per API call (batching ~10 entity-relation tuples per chunk), HippoRAG v2 ~125 sequences per call across three indexed views... Mem0 must embed each extracted fact before its similarity search resolves the ADD/UPDATE/DELETE decision, producing a 1:1 call-to-sequence ratio; agentic systems are similarly sequential.'

headline_numbers.claim: Construction-LLM downscaling has an algorithm-imposed floor
headline_numbers.exact_wording: 'GraphRAG is notably robust, maintaining ~47-48% accuracy across the full ladder from Qwen3-1.7B to GPT-4o-mini... MIRIX fails entirely at Qwen3-1.7B, because its pipeline relies on multiple sub-agent tool calls that require well-formed JSON schemas and legal tool-call syntax; a model that cannot reliably satisfy these contracts produces a corrupted store from which the QA model can recover no useful evidence.'

headline_numbers.claim: The cheapest construction wins on accuracy
headline_numbers.exact_wording: 'BM25 completes construction in under a second and reaches the highest accuracy in the suite at 55.8%, but its query time (~7.4 s) is behind Mem0, A-Mem, and GraphRAG. The structure-augmented and agentic systems pay substantially more construction cost without overtaking BM25 on accuracy: HippoRAG v2 reaches 47.4% at ~277 s of construction, GraphRAG 47.0% at ~2,850 s, and A-Mem 42.1% at ~17,666 s, the most expensive build in the suite. ... Mem0 attains the lowest per-query latency (~2.2 s) by distilling history into atomic facts, but pays ~4,108 s of construction to do so and reaches only 26.8% accuracy. SimpleMem is the slowest at query time (~18.4 s)'
headline_numbers.macro_accuracies_from_Fig_7a: BM25 55.8%, embedRAG 50.3%, HippoRAG v2 47.4%, GraphRAG 47.0%, A-Mem 42.1%, SimpleMem 36.2%, MIRIX 31.7%, Mem0 26.8%, Letta 25.9%

headline_numbers.claim: The authors qualify the BM25 result themselves
headline_numbers.exact_wording: 'BM25's strong aggregate showing should not be read as a universal result. The macro-average in Fig. 7a is computed over all datasets in MemoryAgentBench, many of which are recall-heavy and reward the exact-match retrieval that lexical indexing handles well. BM25 has well-documented weaknesses on queries requiring paraphrase matching, multi-hop reasoning, or temporal inference, the task families that motivate Paradigm III and IV designs. Fig. 7b shows this: the aggregate hides sharp per-category variation, and on the harder categories the gap between BM25 and the structure-augmented systems narrows or reverses.'
headline_numbers.note: this qualifier MUST travel with the 55.8% wherever the book quotes it

headline_numbers.claim: Per-session construction time spans five orders of magnitude and forces a freshness-latency choice
headline_numbers.exact_wording: 'Fig. 8c shows per-session construction time across all papers, spanning five orders of magnitude: from ~10^-3 s for BM25 to ~10 s for Mem0 and MIRIX, with tails exceeding 100 s for inputs that trigger multiple consolidation rounds... the operator faces a forced choice between synchronous scheduling, which exposes construction latency on the critical path, and asynchronous scheduling, which admits unbounded staleness.'
headline_numbers.staleness: under async 5 s inter-session arrival, SimpleMem / MIRIX / Letta / Mem0 / A-Mem accumulate max staleness of 1 or 2 sessions; BM25 and embedRAG stay fresh in both modes

headline_numbers.claim: Per-user footprint and token cost diverge with history length
headline_numbers.exact_wording: 'Per-user memory footprints vary by up to 9x across systems at 1 M tokens, but construction token cost diverges far more sharply. Paradigm IV agentic systems scale super-linearly in LLM token cost as growing memory stores amplify per-ingestion work... An agent's long-term cost is therefore dictated by its algorithmic growth slope, not its initial footprint.' 'Letta in particular diverges steeply beyond 256 K tokens.' 'Retrieval latency (panel d), by contrast, stays nearly flat as the store grows: index-lookup retrieval is sub-linear in store size, decoupling per-query read cost from history length.'

headline_numbers.claim: Tail latency splits by whether the algorithm or the LLM decides when to stop
headline_numbers.exact_wording: 'Algorithm-bounded phases stop at a point fixed by the algorithm: BM25's single top-k lookup, HippoRAG v2's fixed passage-entity-fact-PPR sequence, GraphRAG's one extraction call per chunk... LLM-bounded phases continue until the LLM decides they are done: MIRIX's type-specific tool calls, SimpleMem's reflection rounds, Letta's tool-driven memory access, A-Mem's note evolution. When the specification permits arbitrary depth, only an explicit iteration cap bounds cost.'
headline_numbers.numbers: p95/p50 near 1.3x for BM25 and embedRAG, 1.6x HippoRAG v2, 5.9x GraphRAG, 3.9x Letta

ten_recommendations.gist: treat memory-system selection as a system-level decision; accuracy alone is insufficient
account for energy across the full lifecycle, not just query time

treat construction as a background throughput workload with explicit admission control; rate-limit, batch or defer it away from latency-sensitive QA; Paradigm III.a wants large embedding batches, III.b and IV want per-call latency prioritisation
exploit reuse across overlapping construction inputs — prefix reuse, chunk caching, batching of independent construction units
treat the minimum viable construction LLM as an algorithm-imposed cost floor and validate it before deployment

THE AMORTISATION ONE. Match the construction-versus-query cost split to the query arrival pattern; high query volume against stable histories favours moving work into construction, sparse queries against continuous ingestion favour cheap construction
for inter-session workloads with cross-session dependencies, treat cumulative construction+retrieval time as a hard feasibility constraint
make construction cadence system-aware; consolidating/mutating systems should monitor marginal per-chunk cost and trigger compaction or offline rebuild

evaluate both baseline footprint and cost growth slope; agentic systems need active compaction/summarisation policies; all evaluated systems accumulate monotonically so operators must add independent pruning
treat worst-case latency on both construction and retrieval as a selection criterion; LLM-bounded systems need external iteration caps and timeouts

protocol_modifications_disclosed: 'For dialogue-oriented systems such as SimpleMem, we update the extraction prompts so that they can consume non-dialogue histories and preserve task-relevant facts.' [§3.1, p.4]
'For A-Mem, whose native parser assumes each conversational turn forms a coherent memory note, we aggregate consecutive fine-grained parsed units on non-dialogue datasets.' [§3.1, p.4]
'For Mem0 on in-context-learning datasets, we replace the default personalization-oriented extraction prompt with an ICL-aware prompt that preserves integer labels verbatim.' [§3.1, p.4]

'For Letta with local models, we cap repeated tool calls during construction and retrieval and lightly specialize the system prompt to the task format... the tool-call caps prevent local models from emitting hundreds of duplicate memory tool calls.' [§3.1, p.4]

'At query time, we cap retrieval at 10 memory entries for all systems. In local-model settings with restricted context windows, if a system overflows the context budget, we reduce retrieval to 5 entries; for Letta, we additionally use 512-token ingestion chunks.' [§3.1, p.4]
'Thinking mode is disabled for all calls to avoid context overflow from verbose reasoning traces.' [§3.2, p.5]
'Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-14B use FP8 weight quantization to fit within a single 80 GB serving stack.' [§3.2, p.5]

scale_ceiling.systems: Ten, all $E$-path, across four paradigms. No $W$-path and no $\Theta$-path system is profiled or mentioned.
scale_ceiling.history_length: Primary characterization at 5 x ~360K = 1.8M tokens; scaling study to ~1M tokens for a single user [§4.7, p.10]. This is the paper's genuine reach and it is far beyond anything in the book's corpus — [letta-stc]'s contexts are a few sentences.
scale_ceiling.hardware: ONE NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 per SLURM job. No multi-node, no multi-GPU, no production fleet. 'Multi-node and multi-agent deployments introduce consistency and coordination requirements across distributed memory stores that single-node characterization cannot capture.' [§5, p.11]
scale_ceiling.models: Qwen3-32B / 14B / 8B / 1.7B local (32B and 14B at FP8), GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4.1-mini remote. No model above 32B is served locally, so all energy numbers are for a 32B-class backbone.
scale_ceiling.statistical_scale: n=5 samples and n=20 tasks, no seeds, no error bars, no dispersion of any kind. The statistical footing is no better than the corpus it is measuring.
scale_ceiling.modality: Text only. 'Multimodal memory... is an emerging and less mature frontier that we expect will amplify the construction cost, storage footprint, and retrieval complexity challenges identified here.' [§5, p.11]

book_impact.summary: OVERTURNS: ch26 판정 2's $E$-row magnitude and 표 26-2's '5.5 자릿수' ordering — ch26's own pre-registered falsifier R-1 is met by measurement. THREATENS: ch25's framing and its priority on phase-aware attribution, ch29 §29.3's '$E$-경로가 가장 쉽게 배치된다', ch11/ch13's treatment of condition (1) as an algorithm property. CONFIRMS, some of it strongly: ch25 판정 2 (structural flaw of the amortisation argument), ch25's $\rho$ row, ch25's $N_q$-distribution gap, ch27 판정 2 (E-path is a cost method, not a quality method), ch24/ch23's silence map, ch01's 'offline' false friend. ch28/X3 acquires data with an adverse sign and a new failure mode (capability floor).

overturns.chapter: ch26 — 판정 2 and 표 26-2 (the $E$-row magnitude and the path ordering)
overturns.the_books_sentence_verbatim: '$E$는 콜드다 — 사용자당 수십 KB이고 질의당 한 번 읽힌다.' [ch26 §26.4 판정 2]. And the summary bullet: 'dense-8B 앵커에서 $E$ 56.0 KB → $\Theta$ delta 16.78 MB → $W$ 17.18 GB로 약 5.5 자릿수 벌어지고' [ch26 요약].
overturns.what_contradicts_it: Measured on-disk per-user footprint at a 1M-token single-user history: HippoRAG v2 ~62 MB, Mem0 ~12 MB, embedRAG ~7 MB (derived from the 0.7 TB / 100K-user projection), with a ~9x spread across systems [§4.7, p.10; Fig. 9c, p.10]. 62 MB EXCEEDS the book's own 8B $\Theta$-delta anchor of 16.78 MB.
overturns.the_book_pre-registered_this_exact_falsi: ch26 §26.5 R-1: '세 경로 중 둘 이상의 사용자당 상태를 같은 단위로 인쇄한 보고에서 자릿수 순서가 $E < \Theta_{\text{delta}} < W$가 아닌 경우. 특히 $E$-경로가 임베딩·그래프·다중 인덱스를 누적해 사용자당 저장이 수십 MB를 넘어 $\Theta$ delta 자릿수에 들어오면 표 26-2의 $E$ 행이 무너진다. ... 필요한 관측은 실험이 아니라 인쇄 한 줄이다.' HippoRAG v2 is literally a multi-view graph plus per-view embeddings plus multiple indices, and its per-user store is 62 MB. The observation the book asked for exists.
what_exactly_breaks_and_what_does_not: BREAKS: the absolute $E$ magnitude ('수십 KB'), the 5.5-decade spread, and the strict ordering $E < \Theta_{\text{delta}}$ at realistic history lengths.

SURVIVES: ch26 판정 1 (the category-error verdict) — it is strengthened, because the $E$ number turns out to depend on history length while the $\Theta$ number depends on $r\,d\,L_{\text{layer}}$, which is precisely 판정 1's point. SURVIVES: the TIER assignment ($E$ cold) — Fig. 9d shows retrieval latency stays nearly flat as the store grows, so $E$ is still read once per query from a cold store.

SURVIVES, and this is the honest part: ch26's per-token RATE. [본서 산술] 12 MB / 1M tokens = 12 bytes/token for Mem0, and ch26's own fp32-embedding row is 168 KB / 14,000 tokens = 12 bytes/token. They agree to the digit. What is wrong is not the accounting but the ANCHOR — ch26 anchors $E$ at one 14,000-token conversation, which is 70x below the regime the book is about (long-horizon agents accumulating hundreds of thousands to millions of tokens per user).
overturns.what_ch26_must_do: Rewrite the $E$ row as a RATE (bytes per ingested token, 7–62 depending on store design) rather than a fixed 56.0 KB, restate 판정 2's tier argument without the '수십 KB' magnitude, and record R-1 as MET-by-third-party-measurement rather than as an open falsifier. The 5.5-decade sentence must go or must be re-scoped to a session anchor and labelled as such.

threatens.chapter: ch25 — the framing of 판정 1 and the priority claim of §25.2.3
the_books_sentences_verbatim: '| $L_w$ | ms · TTFT · ITL | **0편**. ms/token도 TTFT도 인쇄된 곳이 없다 |' [ch25 표 25-1]
'이 라인이 systems 독자에게 파는 성질이 정확히 지연인데, 지연의 단위로 잰 값이 없다.' [ch25 §25.2.1]
'corpus 집계가 보인 것은 "잴 수 없다"였다. 그러나 한 자리에서는 잴 수 있다.' [ch25 §25.2.3]
'따라서 "sleep-time compute이 싼가"는 **현재 문헌 상태에서 검증도 반증도 되지 않는다.**' [ch25 §25.4 판정 1]
what_contradicts_it: $L_w$: effective TTFT in seconds is printed for nine $E$-path systems — 0.10 s (Mem0) to 22.58 s (SimpleMem), with totals 0.57 s to 24.68 s — plus p95/p50 tail ratios of 1.2x to 5.9x [Fig. 10, p.10; Fig. 11, p.11; §4.8, pp.10-11]. One of the nine (Mem0) is a discriminant-passer the book reads in ch15.
$B_s$: nine systems' construction cost is printed in kJ, calls and wall-clock on one benchmark and one H100 [Table 3, p.6], with construction wall-clock from <1 min to ~13.3 h [§4.2, p.6].

PHASE ATTRIBUTION: 'We build a phase-aware profiling harness (to be open-sourced) that attributes cost to three logical phases: memory construction, retrieval, and generation. The harness records API telemetry and hardware telemetry on the same monotonic timeline, enabling per-phase attribution of token volume, call structure, latency, utilization, and energy.' [§3.3, p.5], dated 2026-06-04 — two months before this book's S0.
threatens.what_is_and_is_not_broken: The LITERAL claims of ch25 표 25-1 are about the 21 corpus papers' own reporting and are untouched: this paper is not one of the 21, and it is not the ten systems' own papers. What is broken is the INFERENCE the chapter invites — that the quantity is unavailable, that the question is unanswerable, that only this book can measure it. ch25's 'sleep-time compute이 싼가는 현재 문헌 상태에서 검증도 반증도 되지 않는다' must be narrowed to the sleep-time-compute literature and must explicitly except the $E$-path, where a third party has priced ten systems end-to-end in Joules.
threatens.the_falsifier_that_is_now_half_met: ch25 §25.5 항목 6: '세 편 이상의 논문이 $B_s$를 FLOPs로, $C_{\text{cap}}$을 dtype과 함께 세션당 바이트로 인쇄하는 경우. 판정 1의 첫 층위가 corpus 수준에서 무너진다.' This is ONE paper, not three; $B_s$ is in Joules and axis-read tokens, not FLOPs; $C_{\text{cap}}$ is on-disk bytes without dtype. So the falsifier is not formally met — but it is met in substance for the $E$-path, and ch25 cannot leave item 6 standing as though nothing has happened.

threatens.the_books_sentence_verbatim: '그러므로 인프라 관점에서 가장 새로운 요구를 만드는 것은 $W$-경로이고, 가장 큰 자원을 요구하는 것은 $\Theta$-경로이며, **가장 쉽게 배치되는 것은 $E$-경로다**.' [ch29 §29.3 해설]
threatens.what_contradicts_it: Measured, the $E$-path's write path is a heavyweight, contended background job: 13.3 h of construction and 15,429 kJ for 1.8M tokens of history on one H100 (Letta) [Table 3, p.6]; per-session write latency spanning five orders of magnitude, 10^-3 s to >100 s [Fig. 8c, p.9]; construction prefill contending with QA for KV-cache headroom — 'Routing both through the same LLM endpoint means a large construction prefill job occupies KV-cache headroom and stalls the batch scheduler precisely when a latency-sensitive query arrives' [§4.3, p.7]; embedding-server head-of-line blocking by paradigm [§4.3, p.7]; and a forced synchronous-vs-stale scheduling choice when construction exceeds the inter-session interval [Insight 6, p.9].
threatens.what_ch29_must_do: Keep the ordering for the READ path and reverse it for the WRITE path. The $E$-path is the easiest to deploy per query and, for LLM-mediated construction, among the hardest to schedule. ch29 currently has no $E$-path write-path systems section at all; this paper supplies one whole, including a novel resource-contention finding (construction prefill vs latency-sensitive decode on the same stack) that has no analogue in the book.

threatens.chapter: ch11 and ch13 — condition (1) treated as a property of the algorithm
threatens.the_books_sentence_verbatim: 'MemGPT는 쓰기가 **대화 중**에 일어나므로 "질의 전"을 엄밀히 만족하지 않는다.' [PRE-RESEARCH §2.3; ch13 의무 caveat]
threatens.what_contradicts_it: Under this paper's primary protocol the same lineage (Letta, 'Implements the MemGPT [16] abstraction' [§2.2, p.4]) does all of its writing in a batch ingestion phase before any query, and therefore satisfies condition (1). Under §4.6's continuous-arrival protocol, the same system fails to keep up and serves 'against memory one or more sessions behind the ingestion stream' [§4.6, p.9]. The same algorithm sits on both sides of condition (1) depending on how it is driven.
threatens.what_the_book_must_do: ch11 must add one sentence: condition (1) is evaluated against the DEPLOYMENT PROTOCOL, and a system can satisfy it in a batch-construct regime and violate it in a streaming regime. The counting convention (통과 9 + 경계 1 + 불충족 19 = 29) is unaffected because it classifies papers by what the paper does, not deployments — but the boundary-case treatment of MemGPT in ch13 now has an empirical illustration of why it is a boundary and not a wall.
threatens.second_seam: The discriminant's condition (2) as written admits BM25's index build and embedRAG's embedding pass. The inference requirement that actually excludes them lives only in ch10's treatment of RAG. This is the second note in a row to hit that seam (see `memory-survey-2607`). ch11 should promote the inference requirement into the discriminant text.

threatens.chapter: ch28 / experiment X3 — the shape of $B_s$ scaling
threatens.the_threat: X3's plan is to 're-place the reported $B_s$-quality points on a unified axis'. This paper supplies nine such points on ONE benchmark and ONE GPU, and the relation is adverse: the cheapest constructions are the most accurate. Macro-averaged over all MemoryAgentBench: BM25 55.8% at <1 s build, embedRAG 50.3%, HippoRAG v2 47.4% at ~277 s, GraphRAG 47.0% at ~2,850 s, A-Mem 42.1% at ~17,666 s, Mem0 26.8% at ~4,108 s [§4.5, p.8; Fig. 7a, p.9]. On LongMemEval with local Qwen3-32B, ranked by construction energy: embedRAG 495 kJ / 39.8%, BM25 582 kJ / 47.0%, ..., A-Mem 14,864 kJ / 42.7%, Letta 15,429 kJ / 27.7% [Table 3, p.6].
threatens.what_X3_must_do: Separate WITHIN-SYSTEM $B_s$ scaling (e.g. [letta-stc]'s $\kappa_{\parallel}$ sweep, which is a scaling law) from CROSS-SYSTEM $B_s$ comparison (which is a design-choice comparison and has no reason to be monotone). Only the first is a scaling law. This paper's points are all of the second kind and must not be plotted as if they were the first. Carry the authors' own qualifier that the macro-average is recall-heavy and that 'on the harder categories the gap between BM25 and the structure-augmented systems narrows or reverses' [§4.5, p.8].
threatens.a_new_failure_mode_for_the_B_s_axis: The CAPABILITY FLOOR. 'MIRIX fails entirely at Qwen3-1.7B, because its pipeline relies on multiple sub-agent tool calls that require well-formed JSON schemas and legal tool-call syntax; a model that cannot reliably satisfy these contracts produces a corrupted store from which the QA model can recover no useful evidence.' [§4.4, p.8]. $B_s$ is therefore not continuously tradeable: for systems with hard output contracts the quality-vs-$B_s$ curve has a cliff, and below it the store is not degraded but destroyed. ch28 has no such term and should acquire one.

confirms.chapter: ch25 판정 2 — the structural flaw of the amortisation argument
confirms.what: SURVIVES INTACT, and is strengthened from an unexpected direction. This paper has no amortisation identity, no query-count symbol, no break-even, and no read-path token accounting at all; every cost total is at a fixed 60 queries per context. The one quantity ch25/X1 restores — the per-query prompt-token term that is NOT divided by $N_q$ — is absent here too.
confirms.the_stronger_part: ch25 §25.5 반증 조건 3 offers the escape hatch: 'prefill이 실효적으로 공짜인 서빙 구성이 측정으로 제시되는 경우. 판정 2의 실무적 무게가 사라진다.' This paper closes that hatch by assertion from a serving-systems venue: 'Prefix caching mitigates this within active sessions but fails across sessions due to cache eviction and the massive KV-cache memory pressure placed on the serving stack' [§1, p.2]. Since identity (A)'s whole point is reuse ACROSS queries and sessions over one context, this is the regime where the paper says prefix caching does not hold. It is an assertion, not a measurement (the paper never runs with-vs-without prefix caching), so ch25 should cite it as a third-party statement, not as the measurement 반증 3 asks for.
confirms.second_corroboration: ch25 §25.3.1's [해설] argues that a longer prompt buys back in KV bytes what it saves in time, lowering the batch-size ceiling. This paper states the same mechanism from the other side: a construction prefill job 'occupies KV-cache headroom and stalls the batch scheduler' [§4.3, p.7].

confirms.the_books_sentence: '**측정되지 않은 것이 아니라 측정될 실험이 설계되지 않았다.** [본서 관찰]' [ch25 §25.2.1]
confirms.what: Independently confirmed at ten-system scale, with a mechanism-level reason the book does not have: the operator that would produce $\rho$ is not implemented. 'None of the evaluated systems prune or forget by default, so footprint grows monotonically under default behavior' [§4.7, p.10]; 'In many current systems, maintenance is weak or absent: memory accumulates indefinitely with no freshness or pruning policy' [§2.1, p.3]. ch25 can upgrade its 관찰 to a cited fact and ch30 can state that the $\rho$ gap is not a reporting gap but an implementation gap.

confirms.chapter: ch25 §25.3.3 and 반증 조건 5 — the $N_q$ distribution
confirms.what: CONFIRMED, with a fresh instance. Every cost number in this paper is at a fixed 60 queries per context (5 samples x 60 = 300) [§3.1, p.4; Table 3, p.6]. A systems paper with full API and hardware telemetry, whose abstract advertises 'amortization via query volume', reports no $N_q$ distribution and never varies it. ch25's '$N_q$는 방법의 성질이 아니라 워크로드의 성질이다' now has a second witness.

confirms.chapter: ch27 판정 2 — $E$-path is a cost method, not a quality method
confirms.the_books_sentence_verbatim: '$E$-경로는 유망하다. 단 **비용 방법으로서**다. 품질 방법으로서는 현재 문헌이 지지하지 않으며, 그 반증은 이 책이 아니라 논문들 자신의 표에서 나온다.' [ch27 §27.4 판정 2]. And PRE-RESEARCH §1: '$E$-경로에서는 품질 1위가 반복적으로 "기억 시스템 없음"이다.'
confirms.what: THE STRONGEST EXTERNAL EVIDENCE IN THE CORPUS FOR THIS VERDICT. On a ten-system, four-paradigm comparison macro-averaged over all of MemoryAgentBench, the top two are BM25 (55.8%) and embedRAG (50.3%) — the two systems that spend ZERO LLM inference on the write path, i.e. the two that fail the book's own discriminant. The paper states it plainly: 'The structure-augmented and agentic systems pay substantially more construction cost without overtaking BM25 on accuracy' [§4.5, p.8]. The same ordering holds on the local run: BM25 47.0% tops Table 3 [p.6]. Mem0 — the book's own $E$-path passer — comes 8th of 9 on the macro-average at 26.8%.
confirms.how_to_use_it_honestly: The authors' own qualifier is obligatory and must travel with the number: 'BM25's strong aggregate showing should not be read as a universal result... many of which are recall-heavy and reward the exact-match retrieval that lexical indexing handles well... on the harder categories the gap between BM25 and the structure-augmented systems narrows or reverses' [§4.5, p.8]. And the prompt-adaptation caveat (see unfavorable_facts U5) must travel with it too: every system was run in a modified configuration and no adaptation was ablated. With both caveats attached, this is still a far stronger and far more independent instance of the pattern than the single-table baselines ch15 currently cites.

confirms.chapter: ch23 and ch24 — the silence map
confirms.what: A new and sharp specimen. Whole-text counts: 'sleep' 0, 'wake' 0, 'dream' 0, 'hippocamp' 0, 'fast weight' 0, 'LoRA' 0, 'fine-tun' 0, 'TTT' 0, 'Titans' 0. confirms.what: A THIRD sense arrives. `memory-survey-2607` established that in the 2026 architecture literature 'offline' means training-time. Here it means large-batch throughput indexing: 'Embedding traffic splits further by paradigm, between large-batch offline indexing (Paradigm III.a) and sequential per-event writes' [§4.3, p.7]; 'trigger compaction or offline rebuild' [Rec 8, p.9]. ch01's obligation to forbid the bare term now covers three incompatible senses, none of which is the book's 'before the query arrives'.

confirms.chapter: ch11 and ch15 — $\mathrm{wr}$ is the axis that separates $E$-path systems
confirms.what: Table 1's Mutability column classifies $\mathrm{wr}$ three ways — append / consolidate / mutate — as one of four taxonomy axes, produced independently. unfavorable_facts.fact: The paper's own prose contradicts its own table on the headline energy spread, and the headline number cannot be reproduced from the printed data.
unfavorable_facts.detail: §4.2 (p.6) reads 'A-Mem and MIRIX reach 115 kJ and 197 kJ, a 28-47x premium'. Table 3 (p.6) prints A-Mem 116,116 J/correct and MIRIX 144,629 J/correct; Fig. 4's own data labels read 116.1 kJ, 144.6 kJ and 185.9 kJ. The value 197 kJ appears nowhere. Table 3's true max/min is 185,873/4,128 = 45.0x, while Insight 2 and the Fig. 4 caption both state 'exceeds 47x'. The true premium range from the table is 28.1x-35.0x, not 28-47x. The 47x reconciles only with the unsupported 197 kJ.
unfavorable_facts.why_it_bites: the 47x is the paper's single most quotable number and it is not derivable from the paper's only result table
unfavorable_facts.source: [§4.2, p.6; Table 3, p.6; Insight 2, p.6; Fig. 4 caption, p.6]

unfavorable_facts.fact: The energy floor is attributed to the wrong system.
unfavorable_facts.detail: 'BM25 establishes a floor of 4,145 J per correct answer' [§4.2, p.6]. Table 3 prints BM25 = 4,128 and embedRAG = 4,144. Recomputing from the table: 582,000/141 = 4,128 for BM25 and 495,000/119.4 = 4,146 for embedRAG. The quoted floor is embedRAG's value.

unfavorable_facts.why_it_bites: three independent arithmetic errors in one paragraph, all in the direction that makes the spread look larger

unfavorable_facts.fact: The paper's opening quantitative claim is physically implausible and irreconcilable with two of its own later figures.
unfavorable_facts.detail: 'Mem0 achieves <0.1 s per query versus ~38 s for long-context (GPT-4.1-mini, OpenAI API, averaged over 300 queries)' [§4.1, p.6], where Fig. 2's caption defines the axis as 'Per-query serving latency (retrieval + generation, excluding construction)'. A remote GPT-4.1-mini generation call cannot complete inside 0.1 s. §4.5 gives Mem0 ~2.2 s per query and Fig. 10 gives Mem0 0.10 s TTFT against 0.57 s total. The three numbers are never reconciled and the 380x ratio in §4.1 is the paper's motivating figure.

unfavorable_facts.fact: Every system is run in a modified configuration and no modification is ablated.

The paper calls these 'restricted to interface and prompt-level compatibility changes' and ablates none of them.

systems_implications.preamble: Grounding key: [PAPER] = a measured number or a stated claim with a locator; [INFERENCE] = the note-writer's translation. This paper supplies far MORE systems numbers than anything else in the corpus, so the split matters less here than usual — but the inferences drawn for the book are still marked.

items.claim: Construction and QA are two different workloads that must not share a serving endpoint naively. Construction is throughput-oriented, batch, latency-insensitive, prefill-and-embedding-heavy; QA is latency-sensitive and TTFT-optimised.
items.grounding: [PAPER] §4.3, p.7: 'Routing both through the same LLM endpoint means a large construction prefill job occupies KV-cache headroom and stalls the batch scheduler precisely when a latency-sensitive query arrives.' Recommendation 3 asks for rate limiting, batching, deferral and explicit admission control.

items.claim: The embedding server has its own scheduling conflict, and the right policy is paradigm-dependent.
items.grounding: [PAPER] §4.3, p.7: Paradigm III.a submits large batches (GraphRAG ~2,300 sequences per call, HippoRAG v2 ~125), Paradigms III.b and IV are sequential (Mem0 1:1 call-to-sequence). 'An embedding server configured for batch throughput will create head-of-line blocking for latency-sensitive write-loop tenants.'

items.claim: Read-path cost is DECOUPLED from accumulated history; write-path cost is not.
items.grounding: [PAPER] §4.7, p.10: 'Retrieval latency (panel d), by contrast, stays nearly flat as the store grows: index-lookup retrieval is sub-linear in store size, decoupling per-query read cost from history length.' Against this, Paradigm IV construction token cost is super-linear in store size because each ingestion queries the growing store before writing. [INFERENCE] This is the sharpest structural statement about the $E$-path anywhere in the corpus and the book does not have it: the $E$-path's read cost is bounded and its write cost compounds. ch27's 'cost method' verdict should be stated in exactly those terms.

items.claim: Per-user fleet storage is a real capacity problem at scale, but a disk/object-store problem rather than a device-memory one.
items.grounding: [PAPER] §4.7, p.10: 0.7 TB to 6.2 TB per 100K users at 1M tokens each. [INFERENCE] This does NOT create the memory-device opportunity ch29 identifies for $\Theta$ deltas, because the read is once per query from cold storage with flat latency. It does mean ch29's contrast between the two paths must be stated as a difference of TIER and ACCESS PATTERN, not of magnitude — the magnitudes are now comparable.

items.claim: Sleep-phase wall-clock is not free even off the critical path, and the binding constraint is the inter-session interval.
items.grounding: [PAPER] Insight 6, p.9: 'For agent memory systems where per-session construction time exceeds the inter-session arrival interval, synchronous construction scheduling leads to user-facing latency and memory staleness.' Per-session construct time spans 10^-3 s to >100 s [Fig. 8c, p.9]. [INFERENCE] This is the operational form of the question [letta-stc §7] raised and abandoned — 'the length of the sleep-time may also vary significantly between interactions'. The answer for LLM-mediated $E$-path systems is that the sleep interval must exceed tens of seconds per session or the store is permanently behind.

items.claim: Energy, not dollars, is the operator-facing currency, and it makes construction visible in a way latency does not.
items.grounding: [PAPER] §4.2, p.6: 'Energy is invariant: whatever LLM and embedding calls construction makes are paid regardless of when they run. Latency, by contrast, is schedulable.' [INFERENCE] This is a cleaner statement of the sleep/wake asymmetry than the book's — the book prices sleep tokens at $1/\kappa_{\text{cost}}$ of wake tokens, which is a PRICE assumption; energy is invariant to scheduling and needs no such constant. A book that wants to avoid the unmeasured $\kappa_{\text{cost}}$ can use energy instead, and ch25 should say so.

items.claim: Worst-case cost is bounded only where the algorithm bounds it.
items.grounding: [PAPER] §4.8, pp.10-11 and Recommendation 10: algorithm-bounded phases can be provisioned from profiled worst case; LLM-bounded phases 'require external iteration caps and timeouts, since profiling samples the LLM's behavior on tested inputs but does not bound it on others'. p95/p50 1.2-1.3x vs 5.9x. [INFERENCE] [letta-stc]'s $J \le 10$ cap is exactly such an external cap, and the book never noticed that it is a systems requirement rather than an implementation detail.

items.claim: Construction-LLM downscaling is a real cost lever with a discontinuity.
items.grounding: [PAPER] §4.4, p.8: GraphRAG holds ~47-48% from Qwen3-1.7B to GPT-4o-mini; MIRIX fails entirely at Qwen3-1.7B. [INFERENCE] For the book, this is a $B_s$-axis fact with no analogue in the corpus: reducing sleep-time compute by using a smaller model is safe exactly to the point where the write's output contract breaks, and then it is catastrophic rather than gradual.

items.claim: All measurements are on ONE H100 with FP8 for the two largest models and thinking mode disabled.
items.grounding: [PAPER] §3.2, p.5. [INFERENCE] The kJ figures are configuration-specific and must be quoted with the configuration attached; the book's rule of quoting ratios rather than absolutes applies with full force here.
